topics.name: Slope of a Line, Angle Between Two Lines, and Collinearity
topics.summary: The slope of a line measures its steepness: for two points \( (x_1,y_1) \) and \( (x_2,y_2) \), the slope is \( m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1} \), undefined when the line is vertical (\( x_2=x_1 \)) and zero when it is horizontal. The slope equals \( \tan\theta \), where \( \theta \) is the angle the line makes with the positive \( x \)-axis. Given the slopes of two lines, the tangent of the angle between them is \( \tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right| \); this is undefined exactly when \( 1+m_1m_2=0 \), which signals that the lines are perpendicular. Two lines are parallel exactly when their slopes are equal, \( m_1=m_2 \), and perpendicular exactly when the product of their slopes is \( -1 \), i.e. \( m_1m_2=-1 \). Three or more points are collinear exactly when the slope computed between any two pairs of them is the same; this single idea — comparing slopes — underlies tests for collinearity, parallelism, and perpendicularity alike, and is usually the fastest way to characterize how two lines or three points relate to each other.
topics.worked_example: Are the points \( (1,2) \), \( (3,6) \), and \( (5,10) \) collinear? Slope from \( (1,2) \) to \( (3,6) \) is \( m=\frac{6-2}{3-1}=2 \); slope from \( (3,6) \) to \( (5,10) \) is \( m=\frac{10-6}{5-3}=2 \). Since both slopes equal \( 2 \), the three points lie on the same line.
common_mistakes: Swapping the numerator and denominator of the slope formula, computing \( \frac{x_2-x_1}{y_2-y_1} \) instead.
Reversing the order of subtraction in only one of the numerator or denominator, flipping the sign of the slope.
Treating a vertical line's undefined slope as \( 0 \), or a horizontal line's zero slope as undefined.
Checking \( m_1+m_2 \) instead of \( m_1m_2 \) for perpendicularity, or \( m_1=m_2 \) instead of \( m_1m_2=-1 \).
Dropping the absolute value bars in the angle-between-lines formula, or using \( 1-m_1m_2 \) instead of \( 1+m_1m_2 \) in its denominator.

topics.name: Point-Slope and Two-Point Forms of the Equation of a Line
topics.summary: Once the slope of a line is known, its equation can be written directly. The point-slope form \( y-y_1=m(x-x_1) \) builds the equation of a line through a known point \( (x_1,y_1) \) with known slope \( m \). When two points \( (x_1,y_1) \) and \( (x_2,y_2) \) are given instead, the two-point form \( y-y_1=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}(x-x_1) \) first computes the slope between them and then applies the point-slope idea. Both forms produce the same kind of result: an equation that can be rearranged into the general form \( Ax+By+C=0 \). These forms are the natural tool whenever a line is described through the points it passes through — including everyday scenarios such as a ladder leaning against a wall (its foot and the point where it touches the wall) or a straight road passing two landmarks. Once the equation is found, substituting a known \( x \)- or \( y \)-coordinate lets you find the corresponding missing coordinate of any other point on the same line, or check whether a given point lies on it at all.
topics.worked_example: Find the equation of the line through \( (1,2) \) and \( (3,8) \). Slope: \( m=\frac{8-2}{3-1}=3 \). Using the point-slope form at \( (1,2) \): \( y-2=3(x-1) \), which simplifies to \( 3x-y-1=0 \).
common_mistakes: Using the reciprocal of the slope, \( \frac{1}{m} \), in place of \( m \).
Swapping a point's coordinates, using \( (y_1,x_1) \) in place of \( (x_1,y_1) \).
Making a sign slip on the constant term while clearing fractions.
Swapping the roles of the \( x \)- and \( y \)-differences (effectively using the reciprocal slope) when applying the two-point form.
Omitting the negative sign when isolating \( y \) (or \( x \)) from \( Ax+By+C=0 \).

topics.name: Slope-Intercept Form and Intercept Form of the Equation of a Line
topics.summary: The slope-intercept form \( y=mx+c \) directly displays a line's slope \( m \) and its \( y \)-intercept \( c \) (where the line crosses the \( y \)-axis). The intercept form \( \frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1 \) instead displays both axis intercepts at once: \( a \) is where the line crosses the \( x \)-axis, and \( b \) is where it crosses the \( y \)-axis. The two forms convert into each other easily — from \( y=mx+c \), setting \( y=0 \) gives the \( x \)-intercept \( a=-\frac{c}{m} \), while \( b=c \). A particularly useful application of the intercept form is finding the area of the triangle a line forms with the coordinate axes: with legs \( |a| \) and \( |b| \) along the two axes, the area is \( \frac{1}{2}|ab| \). This connects a line's equation directly to a simple geometric quantity, and problems often run the idea in reverse — given the area and one intercept, find the other, or given a condition relating the two intercepts (such as their sum), find the equation itself.
topics.worked_example: A line has \( x \)-intercept \( a=4 \) and \( y \)-intercept \( b=6 \). Its equation in intercept form is \( \frac{x}{4}+\frac{y}{6}=1 \), and the triangle it forms with the axes has area \( \frac{1}{2}|4\times 6|=12 \).
common_mistakes: Swapping the slope and the \( y \)-intercept, or swapping the \( x \)-intercept and \( y \)-intercept.
Omitting the negative sign when finding the \( x \)-intercept from \( y=mx+c \), using \( \frac{c}{m} \) instead of \( -\frac{c}{m} \).
Omitting the factor of \( \frac{1}{2} \), or the absolute value, in the triangle-area formula \( \frac{1}{2}|ab| \).
Inverting the relationship between the intercepts and the area when solving for an unknown intercept.

topics.name: Normal Form of the Equation of a Line
topics.summary: The normal form of a line's equation, \( x\cos\omega+y\sin\omega=p \), describes a line by the length \( p \) of the perpendicular dropped from the origin to the line, and the angle \( \omega \) that perpendicular makes with the positive \( x \)-axis, with the conventions \( p>0 \) and \( 0\leq\omega<2\pi \). To convert a general equation \( Ax+By+C=0 \) into this form, divide every term by \( r=\sqrt{A^2+B^2} \), choosing the sign of the division (i.e. dividing by \( r \) or by \( -r \)) so that the resulting constant on the right-hand side is positive — this is what guarantees \( p>0 \). The value of \( p \) obtained this way is exactly the perpendicular distance of the origin from the line, so the normal form gives this distance immediately, without needing a separate formula. Because \( \cos\omega \) and \( \sin\omega \) must come from an actual angle, they automatically satisfy \( \cos^2\omega+\sin^2\omega=1 \), which is a useful check on any claimed normal form.
key_formulas: \( r=\sqrt{A^2+B^2} \), with the sign chosen so \( p>0 \)
topics.worked_example: Reduce \( 3x+4y-10=0 \) to normal form. Here \( r=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5 \). Since the constant term is \( -10 \) (negative), dividing by \( r=5 \) (not \( -5 \)) keeps the result positive: \( \frac{3}{5}x+\frac{4}{5}y=2 \), so \( \cos\omega=\frac{3}{5} \), \( \sin\omega=\frac{4}{5} \), \( p=2 \).
common_mistakes: Dividing by the wrong sign of \( r \), which flips both \( \cos\omega \) and \( \sin\omega \) and can leave \( p \) negative.
Swapping \( \cos\omega \) and \( \sin\omega \) (mixing up the coefficients of \( x \) and \( y \)).
Reporting \( p \) with the wrong sign, violating the requirement that \( p>0 \).
Forgetting to also multiply \( p \) by \( r \) when clearing the normal form back to general form.

topics.name: General Equation of a Line and Conversion to Standard Forms
topics.summary: The general equation \( Ax+By+C=0 \) is the common form every line can be written in, and every other form (point-slope, two-point, slope-intercept, intercept, normal) can be converted into it or read out of it. From \( Ax+By+C=0 \) directly: the slope is \( m=-\frac{A}{B} \), the \( x \)-intercept is \( -\frac{C}{A} \), and the \( y \)-intercept is \( -\frac{C}{B} \). Two lines \( A_1x+B_1y+C_1=0 \) and \( A_2x+B_2y+C_2=0 \) are parallel exactly when \( A_1B_2-A_2B_1=0 \) (equivalently, \( \frac{A_1}{A_2}=\frac{B_1}{B_2} \)), and perpendicular exactly when \( A_1A_2+B_1B_2=0 \). These coefficient-based conditions are often faster than first converting to slope-intercept form. They are also the key to constructing a new line through a given point that is parallel or perpendicular to a given line: a parallel line keeps the same \( A \) and \( B \), while a perpendicular line replaces them with \( -B \) and \( A \); either way, substituting the given point then pins down the new constant term \( C \).
topics.worked_example: For the line \( 6x-2y+5=0 \), the slope is \( m=-\frac{6}{-2}=3 \), the \( x \)-intercept is \( -\frac{5}{6} \), and the \( y \)-intercept is \( -\frac{5}{-2}=\frac{5}{2} \).
common_mistakes: Omitting the negative sign in \( m=-\frac{A}{B} \), or in the intercept formulas \( -\frac{C}{A} \) and \( -\frac{C}{B} \).
Swapping the \( x \)-intercept and \( y \)-intercept.
Using the wrong coefficient condition for the wrong relationship — checking \( A_1A_2+B_1B_2 \) for parallelism, or \( A_1B_2-A_2B_1 \) for perpendicularity.
Using the perpendicular-direction coefficients \( -B,A \) when a parallel line was wanted through a given point, or vice versa.

topics.name: Distance of a Point From a Line and Distance Between Parallel Lines
topics.summary: The perpendicular distance of a point \( (x_1,y_1) \) from a line \( Ax+By+C=0 \) is \( d=\frac{|Ax_1+By_1+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}} \); the absolute value bars are essential, since a distance is never negative regardless of which side of the line the point lies on. When two lines are parallel, they share the same coefficients \( A \) and \( B \) (after suitably scaling one equation to match the other, if necessary), and the distance between them is \( d=\frac{|C_1-C_2|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}} \). Because this formula only applies once the coefficients truly match, the first step with two parallel lines given in different scalings is always to divide one equation through so that its \( x \)- and \( y \)-coefficients agree exactly with the other's. Both formulas appear naturally in word problems — the distance from a point to a modeled straight path, or the width of a strip between two parallel boundaries — and also in reverse problems, where an unknown coordinate or constant is found by setting a known distance equal to the formula and solving.
common_mistakes: Omitting the absolute value bars, leaving a signed (possibly negative) result instead of a positive distance.
Forgetting to divide by \( \sqrt{A^2+B^2} \) entirely.
Omitting the constant term \( C \) when substituting into the numerator.
Using \( C_1+C_2 \) instead of \( C_1-C_2 \) in the parallel-lines distance formula.
Applying the parallel-lines distance formula before scaling the two equations so their coefficients actually match.

questions.question: Quadrilateral \( PQRS \) has \( P \)=(2, -8), \( Q \)=(-1, 3), \( R \)=(-1, 8), \( S \)=(8, 0). Are the diagonals \( PR \) and \( QS \) perpendicular? Also give the equation of diagonal \( PR \) in intercept form.
questions.explanation: Slope of \( PR \) is \( m_1=-\frac{16}{3} \) and slope of \( QS \) is \( m_2=-\frac{1}{3} \); since \(m_1m_2\neq -1\), the diagonals are not perpendicular. Diagonal \( PR \)'s equation is \( 16x+3y-8=0 \), i.e. \( \frac{x}{\frac{1}{2}}+\frac{y}{\frac{8}{3}}=1 \) in intercept form.
questions.hint: Compute both diagonals' slopes and check \( m_1m_2=-1 \); separately, convert diagonal \( PR \)'s equation to intercept form.

questions.question: A ladder leans against a wall (the \( y \)-axis), with its foot at (5, 0) and top at (0, 12) on the ground/wall axes. A cat is sitting at (4, 6). Find the equation of the line along the ladder, and the cat's perpendicular distance from it.
questions.explanation: The ladder's equation (through the foot and top) is \( 12x+5y-60=0 \). With \( r=13 \), the cat's distance is \( d=\frac{|(12)(4)+(5)(6)+(-60)|}{13}=\frac{18}{13} \).
questions.hint: Form the ladder's equation with the two-point form, then apply the point-to-line distance formula for the cat's position.

questions.topic: Slope-Intercept Form and Intercept Form of the Equation of a Line
questions.question: Find the equation, in intercept form, of the line parallel to \( -5x+4y-3=0 \) whose \( x \)-intercept is \( -3 \).
questions.explanation: A line parallel to \( -5x+4y-3=0 \) has the same \( A,B \): \( -5x+4y+C_2=0 \). Substituting the \( x \)-intercept \( (-3,0) \) gives \( C_2=-15 \), and the \( y \)-intercept is \( b=-\frac{C_2}{B}=\frac{15}{4} \), so the intercept form is \( \frac{x}{-3}+\frac{y}{\frac{15}{4}}=1 \).
questions.hint: A parallel line keeps the same \( A,B \); substitute the given \( x \)-intercept to solve for the new constant, then find the \( y \)-intercept.
